summary: Sucralfate is a locally acting mucosal protectant used for short-term treatment and maintenance of duodenal ulcer. It forms an adherent complex with proteinaceous exudate at the ulcer site, shielding it from acid, pepsin and bile salts. It is minimally absorbed and acts topically rather than systemically.
indications: Short-term treatment (up to 8 weeks) of active duodenal ulcer
Maintenance therapy for duodenal ulcer at reduced dosage after healing

dosage.d: 1 g four times daily on an empty stomach
dosage.n: Healing may occur in 1-2 weeks but continue until confirmed
Reduced dosage after acute ulcer healing

dosage.d: Start at low end of dosing range

admin: Take on an empty stomach (1 hour before meals and at bedtime)
Do not take antacids within 30 minutes before or after sucralfate
Separate other oral medications by at least 2 hours to avoid binding
Not for intravenous administration (fatal emboli reported)
moa: Forms an ulcer-adherent complex with proteinaceous exudate at the ulcer site, creating a physical barrier against acid, pepsin and bile salts. Also inhibits pepsin activity, adsorbs bile salts and has modest acid-neutralizing capacity (~14-16 mEq per 1 g).

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to sucralfate or any excipient
relative: Conditions predisposing to bezoar formation (e.g. delayed gastric emptying, enteral feeding)
monitor: Aluminium levels in chronic renal failure

preg: Teratogenicity studies in mice, rats and rabbits at up to 50 times the human dose revealed no fetal harm. No adequate well-controlled human studies; use during pregnancy only if clearly needed.
lact: It is not known whether sucralfate is excreted in human milk. Because many drugs are excreted in human milk, exercise caution when administering to a nursing woman.
renal: Minimal systemic absorption, but absorbed aluminium is renally excreted. Caution in renal impairment and avoid in dialysis/severe failure due to risk of aluminium accumulation and toxicity.
hepatic: No specific adjustment. Cautious dosing recommended in the elderly who may have reduced hepatic function.

interactions.food: Take on an empty stomach; food may reduce ulcer-adherent binding
interactions.alcohol: No specific interaction; avoid mucosa-irritating intake
interactions.diagnostics: May reduce absorption of co-administered drugs - separate dosing by 2 hours

rare: Diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, gastric discomfort, dry mouth
emergency: Pulmonary or cerebral emboli (if inadvertently injected)

monitoring: Ulcer healing (endoscopy or x-ray as indicated)
Signs of bezoar in predisposed patients
counsel: Take on an empty stomach, 1 hour before meals and at bedtime
Separate antacids by at least 30 minutes
Separate other medicines by at least 2 hours
Increase fluid and fibre intake to reduce constipation
Complete the full course even if symptoms improve
pk: Local action begins promptly on contact with ulcer
Store at 20-25 C (68-77 F), controlled room temperature
pearls: Acts locally - systemic effects are minimal
Major practical issue is binding/reducing absorption of other oral drugs
Avoid in dialysis patients due to aluminium load
Requires acidic environment - efficacy may fall with concurrent antacids
missed: Take the missed dose as soon as remembered. If it is near the next scheduled dose, skip it; do not double up.
overdose: Experience is limited; sucralfate is minimally absorbed so risk is low. Most patients remain asymptomatic; reported symptoms include dyspepsia, abdominal pain, nausea and vomiting. Provide supportive care.
